title: Japji 28–33, whole
hookLine: the yogi's true ornaments and the ladder
tomorrow: a ladder needs a top. what are the five floors up there?

cards: Simran is rehearsing the send-off speech to the bathroom mirror in Maya's big gold hoops, because looking confident is half of it, right? Nanak met people who dressed the part too.
The yogis of his day wore large earrings, carried a begging pouch, smeared ash on their skin. Pauri 28 doesn't mock any of it.
It moves it inside: make contentment your earrings, modesty your pouch, meditation your ash, faith your staff. Then comes the strange part.
A few pauris on, the Japji hands you a ladder, and right after that, says you have no power to climb.

teach.b: Start with a word you've been saying for days. Each stanza of the Japji is a pauri, and in everyday Punjabi a pauri is a step, a stair. So the whole hymn is already built like a staircase.

teach.h: THE WHOLE HUMAN RACE, YOUR ORDER.
teach.b: Pauri 28 adds a line worth carrying out of the room: make the whole human race your order. The yogis belonged to orders; Nanak's order is everyone. Pauri 29: let wisdom be your food, and compassion the one who serves it.
If my one tongue became a hundred thousand tongues, I would say the Name on every one, and these are the steps of the ladder; climb them, and you become one with the One. Now the puzzle.

teach.h: NO POWER TO SPEAK OR BE SILENT.
teach.b: Pauri 33 opens: no power to speak, no power to be silent. No power to ask, or to give, or to live, or to die. The power is in that hand alone.
So why the ladder? Here's a way to solve it. The steps aren't feats of strength.
They're the Name, said and said again, the same small step a hundred thousand times. Pauri 33 just won't let you sign your name under the climb. You keep stepping.
The holding isn't yours. Simran takes the hoops off, then puts them back on. She writes contentment on a sticky note and sticks it to the mirror.

how: Pauris 28 to 33 are recited as part of the Japji in the morning Nitnem; some Sikhs repeat Waheguru as simran, and teachers often point to pauri 32's ladder when they explain why the Name is said again and again.

o: a rule about which earrings a yogi is allowed to wear
the stretch where ornaments go inside and a ladder appears
the hymn Sikhs say only after taking amrit

games.q: the ornaments and the ladder — tap the pairs.
p: the one who serves wisdom's food
no power to speak or be silent

s: in pauri 28 Nanak tells the yogis to throw their earrings away
he moves the ornaments inside: let contentment be your earrings, modesty your pouch, meditation your ash.
pauri 28 says to make the whole human race your order
the yogis belonged to orders. Nanak's order is everyone.
pauri 33 says enough practice gives you power over life and death
it says there is no power to live or die, to speak or be silent; the power is in the One's hand.

games.q: a new club at school fills up with kids from one background, and someone says it should stay 'just our people.' what does pauri 28 suggest?
o: count the whole human race as your order, and keep the door open.
keep it close; an order is for people who already share your path.
skip clubs; real contentment means you never need a group at all.
games.why: Nanak doesn't tell the yogis to stop belonging. he widens the order: make the whole human race your company.

practice: Sit the way a yogi might, back straight, hands open on your knees, chin level. With each slow breath out, settle one of pauri 28's ornaments: contentment, then modesty, then faith, and start again.
Let the posture hold you; you don't have to.

wordCard.voice: Japji 28: the start of pauris 28 to 33, where the yogi's ornaments move inside and the Japji hands you a ladder made of the Name.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: a step or stair, and the name of each stanza of the Japji. the hymn is a staircase before pauri 32 even mentions a ladder.

carryVoice: For the road: the ladder, one small step of the Name at a time, held by a hand that isn't yours. Hoops on, sticky note up.
